client: I lost my dad about two months ago, and honestly, things have been really hard since then. Every time I go to a family gathering, it just hits me all over again — like this wave of sadness that I can't push down, no matter how much I try to hold it together. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep feeling this way.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your father — what you're carrying right now is incredibly heavy, and the way grief resurfaces at family gatherings makes complete sense, because those are the moments that remind you most of who's missing. I can hear in the way you're speaking that you're holding a lot of pain quietly, almost like you've been trying to contain something that's too big to contain. The fact that you're here and willing to try, even when you're not sure it will help, actually takes a lot of courage — and that's a meaningful first step we can build on together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure "courage" is the right word for it. It feels more like desperation, honestly — like I've run out of other options and I didn't know what else to do. I've been holding it together for everyone else at these family things, and I just... I'm exhausted from pretending he's not gone.
therapist: What you're describing — that bone-deep exhaustion from being the one who holds it together for everyone else — is one of the heaviest parts of grief, and it makes complete sense that you've reached a point where you simply can't keep carrying it alone. The way you're speaking right now, softly and carefully, tells me you're running on empty, and "desperation" is actually a really honest and valid place to be. In CBT we'd gently ask: what would it mean for you to *stop* pretending, even just in this space — what are you afraid might happen if you let yourself feel it fully?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what scares me most is that if I actually let myself feel it fully, I won't be able to stop. Like there's this wall I've built and if I let even one crack form, the whole thing just collapses and I'll fall apart completely, and then who takes care of everything? My mom's funeral arrangements still aren't finished, my brother is useless, and I'm the one everyone calls when they need something, so I can't afford to fall apart right now.
therapist: That fear of "falling apart completely" is one of the most common and painful beliefs that grieving people carry, especially those who've taken on the role of caregiver for everyone else — but I want to gently offer a different perspective: feeling grief fully doesn't actually mean losing control forever, it usually comes in waves that *do* pass, even when it doesn't feel that way. I notice you're speaking quickly and your voice is soft, like you're holding your breath while carrying an enormous weight, and that tells me the pressure you're under is very real right now. What if "falling apart" and "taking care of things" weren't actually opposites — what if allowing yourself to grieve, even in small moments, could give you *more* capacity to keep going rather than less?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but honestly, it sounds a little too neat, like something that works for other people but maybe not for me. Every time I've let myself feel even a little bit of the grief about losing my mom, it's like I can't stop thinking about all the things I still need to handle — the estate, my siblings calling me for answers, the bills — and it just pulls me right back into crisis mode. I'm scared that if I actually let myself sit with it, even for a small moment, everything I've been holding together will just... unravel.
therapist: Your skepticism makes complete sense — it would feel hollow to accept a neat idea when your lived experience keeps pulling you straight back into survival mode the moment grief surfaces, and I hear that this isn't just fear, it's something you've actually tested and felt fail you. The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with a kind of tension in your voice — tells me you're in that crisis mode even as we talk, like part of you is already bracing for the next thing that needs handling. I want to sit with that for a moment rather than rush past it: you've been in emergency mode for so long that stillness itself has started to feel like the danger — and that's something we can work with gently, at a pace that feels safe for *you*, not for some textbook version of grief.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, you're right that I'm tense right now, I can feel it in my chest even just sitting here talking about it. And honestly, the idea of working with that "gently" sounds nice in theory, but I've been in this mode for so long I'm not even sure I'd recognize what calm feels like.
therapist: The fact that you can feel that tension physically in your chest right now is actually really important information — your body has been on high alert for so long that it's forgotten what "off" feels like, and that's not a personal failing, that's what prolonged crisis does to a nervous system. I can hear it in how you're speaking right now — there's a quickness, an alertness, like part of you is still scanning for the next emergency even in this room. So rather than asking you to find "calm" — which might feel completely foreign right now — what if we just started by noticing what *slightly less tense* might feel like, just one small degree of difference, because that might be a more honest and reachable place to begin?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, part of me appreciates that you're not just telling me to "calm down" because I've heard that a hundred times and it never helps. But I'm not sure I even know what "slightly less tense" would feel like — like, how do I notice a difference when the tension has just been... there, constantly, for so long that it feels like it's just me? I guess what I'm also thinking is, even if I could find that small degree of difference in here, the second I walk out that door, the phone might ring with another problem and it all just snaps back anyway.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, with a kind of urgency — actually *shows* what you're describing, like your body is demonstrating the very thing we're talking about, and I want to name that not as a problem but as useful information. You've raised something really important though: what's the point of finding relief in here if it evaporates the moment real life hits? That's not resistance — that's a genuinely smart question, and it points to the real work, which isn't about creating a bubble of calm that shatters outside, but about slowly building a slightly different relationship with the tension so it has a little less power over you, even when the phone does ring.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I appreciate that you're not just brushing off my question. But "a slightly different relationship with the tension" — I don't even know what that looks like in practice, because when my phone rings and it's my boss, my whole body just goes into this mode where I can't think straight. It's like all the calm reasoning just gets wiped out instantly, and I'm back to feeling like I'm about to get fired or like I've done something wrong even when I probably haven't.
therapist: What you're describing — that instant full-body hijack when your boss calls, where all rational thought just vanishes — is actually a really well-understood pattern in CBT, where your nervous system has learned to treat certain triggers as threats and responds before your thinking mind even has a chance to catch up. I notice you're speaking quickly and softly, like even describing this puts you back on edge, which tells me this isn't just a thought pattern — it's deeply physical and automatic, and that's important to acknowledge. The practical work here wouldn't be about staying calm *during* the moment, but about gently examining what your mind is telling you in that split second — because you said it yourself: you probably *haven't* done anything wrong, which means there's a story your nervous system is telling you that we could start to look at together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I was going to say... examining the story my mind tells me sounds fine in theory, but my mind is telling me a story that feels completely true, not like some distortion I invented. therapist: You're making a really important distinction, and I want to be clear: you're absolutely right that your loneliness is real, and CBT isn't about talking you out of genuine pain or pretending hard things aren't happening. What I notice is that even as you're saying this, your voice has a kind of urgency and tension to it, like you're bracing for me to dismiss what you're feeling — and I want you to know I'm not going to do that. The goal isn't to replace the truth with something rosier, but to make sure the story doesn't *expand beyond* the facts — because "I haven't talked to a friend in weeks" is real, but there may be a difference between that fact and what your mind then concludes about what it *means* about you and your future.

client: I guess I can see what you're saying, but it's hard not to feel like the conclusions my mind jumps to are just... obvious. therapist: The conclusion feels obvious to you — but I want to gently press on one thing: you've just told me you've been the person everyone calls, the one managing estates and siblings and crises for months, so is it possible that the silence from friends reflects how consumed and unavailable *life* has made you, rather than where you stand in people's hearts? I can hear something in your voice right now — a kind of strained, high-pitched quality, like you're speaking quickly to stay ahead of the pain — and it makes me wonder if part of you is actually hoping I'll push back on this conclusion rather than confirm it. The meaning that feels "obvious" to an exhausted, grieving mind that hasn't had a real conversation in weeks deserves to be questioned, not because your pain isn't real, but because exhaustion and grief are not reliable narrators.
